Module Documentation

tasks.py

Description of the machine-learning task a PARROT network is trained for.

Every PARROT network maps a protein sequence either to a single value (sequence-mapped data) or to one value per residue (residue-mapped data), and that value is either a class label (classification) or a real number (regression). A Task bundles these two choices so that the rest of the code can pass around one object instead of separate datatype / problem-type / number-of-classes arguments.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

  • num_classes (int) – Number of classes for a classification task, or 1 for a regression task.

architectures

Network architectures available to PARROT.

Each architecture lives in its own module in this package and registers itself with register_architecture. Importing this package imports every built-in architecture, so they are all available by name to the command-line tools.

To add a new architecture, see docs/adding_architectures.rst.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

class parrot.architectures.HyperParameter(name: str, value_type: type[int] | type[float] | type[str], default: bool | int | float | str, help: str, cli_aliases: tuple[str, ...] = (), minimum: int | float | None = None, maximum: int | float | None = None, choices: tuple[bool | int | float | str, ...] | None = None, search_range: tuple[int | float, int | float] | None = None, log_scale: bool = False, legacy_value: bool | int | float | str | None = None, search_choices: tuple[bool | int | float | str, ...] | None = None)[source]

Declaration of a single hyperparameter.

Hyperparameters are numbers (int or float), on/off switches (bool), or text with a fixed set of allowed choices (e.g. a pooling method).

A bool hyperparameter’s command-line flag switches it away from its default: ‘–<name>-off’ for one that is on by default (e.g. ‘–attention-pooling-off’), ‘–<name>’ for one that is off by default.

Parameters:

  • name (str) – Python identifier for the hyperparameter (e.g. ‘hidden_size’). The command-line flag is derived from it (e.g. ‘–hidden-size’).

  • value_type (type) – int, float, bool or str. A str hyperparameter must declare choices.

  • default (int, float or str) – Value used when none is provided. Must itself be a valid value.

  • help (str) – One-line description shown in command-line help.

  • cli_aliases (tuple of str, optional) – Additional command-line flags (e.g. (‘-hs’,)).

  • minimum (int or float, optional) – Smallest allowed value (inclusive). None means no lower bound.

  • maximum (int or float, optional) – Largest allowed value (inclusive). None means no upper bound.

  • choices (tuple, optional) – The only values allowed. Required for str hyperparameters.

  • search_range (tuple of (int or float), optional) – Inclusive (low, high) range searched by hyperparameter optimisation (parrot-optimize), for numeric hyperparameters. None means the range is not searched.

  • log_scale (bool, optional) – If True the optimiser searches this hyperparameter on a log10 scale.

  • search_choices (tuple, optional) – The values hyperparameter optimisation tries, for hyperparameters with a fixed set of values (choices, or True/False). None means they are not searched. A hyperparameter has either a search_range or search_choices.

  • legacy_value (int, float, str or bool, optional) – The value used for networks saved before this hyperparameter existed, if that differs from default (e.g. a feature that is now on by default but that older networks did not have), so they are rebuilt exactly as they were trained. None means such networks use the default.

property cli_flag: str

The long command-line flag for this hyperparameter, e.g. ‘–hidden-size’ or ‘–attention-pooling-off’.

property searchable: bool

True if hyperparameter optimisation should search over this hyperparameter.

validate(value: Any) → bool | int | float | str[source]

Convert a value to this hyperparameter’s type and check it is allowed.

Parameters:

value (int, float, str or bool) – The value to check

Returns:

The value converted to value_type

Return type:

int, float, str or bool

Raises:

ValueError – If the value is the wrong type, cannot be represented exactly as value_type (e.g. 2.5 for an integer hyperparameter), is outside [minimum, maximum], or is not one of choices.

class parrot.architectures.ParrotArchitecture(input_size: int, task: Task, hyperparameter_values: Mapping[str, bool | int | float | str])[source]

Base class for every PARROT network architecture.

To add a new architecture, subclass this class, set the three class attributes below, implement __init__ and forward, and decorate the class with parrot.architectures.register_architecture.

__init__ must accept input_size and task followed by one keyword argument per declared hyperparameter, and must pass the hyperparameter values up to this class so they are saved alongside the network weights.

forward(x, lengths) receives a zero-padded batch x of shape [batch_dim X padded_length X input_size] and the true length of each sequence (or None if the batch is unpadded). It must return a tensor of shape [batch_dim X num_classes] for sequence-mapped tasks or [batch_dim X padded_length X num_classes] for residue-mapped tasks, and the output for a sequence must not depend on how much padding it was given. For classification the outputs are unnormalised logits.

Variables:

  • name (str) – Registry key used to select the architecture (e.g. ‘brnn’).

  • description (str) – One-line description shown in command-line help.

  • hyperparameters (tuple of HyperParameter) – The architecture’s hyperparameters.

  • supported_datatypes (tuple of str) – The datatypes (‘sequence’, ‘residues’) the architecture can be used for. Defaults to both.

  • trained_by_gradient_descent (bool) – True (default) for networks trained epoch by epoch with a learning rate. False for models fitted in a single step (see architectures/classical.py).

  • input_size (int) – Length of the per-residue encoding vectors.

  • task (Task) – The task this network was built for.

  • hyperparameter_values (dict) – The hyperparameter values this network was built with.

forward(x: Tensor, lengths: Tensor | None = None) → Tensor[source]

Map a batch of encoded sequences to outputs (see the class docstring).

property num_classes: int

Number of output values per sequence (or per residue).

Return type:

dict

Raises:

ValueError – If a value is given for a hyperparameter the architecture does not have, or a value is invalid.

The interface every PARROT network architecture implements.

An architecture is a PyTorch module that takes a zero-padded batch of encoded sequences (plus the true length of each sequence) and returns either one output vector per sequence or one output vector per residue, depending on the task. Each architecture also declares its hyperparameters, which is what lets the command-line tools build flags for them and the optimiser search over them without knowing anything else about the architecture.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

parrot.architectures.registry.fill_legacy_values(architecture_class: type[ParrotArchitecture], values: Mapping[str, Any]) → dict[str, Any][source]

Complete the saved hyperparameter values of a network with any hyperparameters added since it was saved

A hyperparameter added to PARROT after a network was saved is missing from the values saved with it. If the hyperparameter declares a legacy_value (the behaviour networks had before it existed), that value is used, so the network is rebuilt exactly as it was trained; other missing hyperparameters are left to take their defaults.

Parameters:

  • architecture_class (subclass of ParrotArchitecture) – The saved network’s architecture

  • values (dict) – The hyperparameter values saved with the network

Returns:

values, plus the legacy value of every missing hyperparameter that has one

Return type:

dict

Building blocks shared by several architectures, mostly for handling padding.

PARROT batches sequences of different lengths by zero-padding them at the end, and every architecture must give the same output for a sequence however much padding it was given. The helpers here make that easy: build a mask of the real residues, re-apply it after any layer that could write into padded positions, normalise each position independently, and pool only over real residues.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

class parrot.architectures.layers.AttentionPool(channels: int)[source]

Pool per-residue features into one vector per sequence with learned attention weights

Attention-based pooling (Ilse et al. 2018, ICML): each real residue gets a score w . tanh(V h), a softmax over the sequence’s real residues turns the scores into weights, and the pooled vector is the weighted average of the residue features. Unlike the mean, the network learns which residues matter; unlike the maximum, every residue contributes. Padded positions get zero weight.

[batch_dim X channels]

torch.Tensor

class parrot.architectures.layers.GlobalContext(channels: int)[source]

A summary of the whole sequence, to be added to every position of a channel-first batch

The summary is the average of the features over the sequence’s real positions, passed through a linear layer (as in global-context and squeeze-and-excitation networks: Hu et al. 2018, CVPR; Cao et al. 2019, ICCV Workshops). Added to every position, it lets a convolutional network see the whole sequence however long it is. The linear layer starts at zero, so a new network starts out exactly as it would without the summary.

The bidirectional LSTM network that PARROT has always used.

For sequence-mapped tasks the final hidden states of the forward and reverse directions are concatenated (by default with log(sequence length)) and passed through a linear layer (“many-to-one”). For residue-mapped tasks the linear layer is applied to the LSTM output at every residue (“many-to-many”).

parrot.architectures.brnn.run_lstm(lstm: LSTM, x: Tensor, lengths: Tensor | None = None) → tuple[Tensor, Tensor][source]

Run a batch_first bidirectional LSTM over a (possibly zero-padded) batch of sequences

Sequences in a batch are zero-padded at the end up to the length of the longest sequence. If the LSTM simply ran over those padding positions, the reverse direction would start inside the padding, so a sequence’s output would depend on which other sequences it was batched with. When lengths is given, each direction is run separately on unpacked tensors (run_lstm_unpacked) so the LSTM sees only the real residues of each sequence. This gives the same result, to floating-point precision, as packing the batch with pack_padded_sequence, but is faster on every device: packed sequences are ~1.7x slower on the CPU, ~16x slower on Apple-silicon GPUs (MPS), and up to ~7x slower on NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA), where the gap grows with sequence length.

Parameters:

  • lstm (torch.nn.LSTM) – A bidirectional LSTM constructed with batch_first=True

  • x (torch.Tensor) – Input batch in the format [batch_dim X padded_length X input_size]

  • lengths (torch.Tensor, optional) – The true (unpadded) length of each sequence in the batch. If None, every position of x is treated as a real residue (i.e. no padding).

Returns:

  • torch.Tensor – Per-position LSTM output in the format [batch_dim X padded_length X hidden_size*2]. Padded positions are zero.

  • torch.Tensor – Final hidden state of each layer and direction, in the format [num_layers*2 X batch_dim X hidden_size] (ordered as torch.nn.LSTM orders them), taken at each sequence’s true final residue.

parrot.architectures.brnn.run_lstm_unpacked(lstm: LSTM, x: Tensor, lengths: Tensor) → tuple[Tensor, Tensor][source]

run_lstm() without packing, by running each direction of each layer separately

The forward direction can run straight over the padded batch: its output at a real residue only depends on the residues before it, and the padding comes after every real residue. For the reverse direction, each sequence is reversed within its own length (the padding stays at the end), run forwards, and reversed back. Layers are computed one at a time because each layer’s input is both directions of the layer below. The result equals running the bidirectional LSTM on packed sequences.

The weights are always the bidirectional lstm’s own parameters, so saved networks are unaffected; each direction is computed by calling a weightless single-layer LSTM with those parameters (torch.func.functional_call).

Parameters:

lstm, x, lengths – As for run_lstm()

Return type:

As for run_lstm()

An order-independent baseline: predictions from residue composition alone.

For sequence-mapped tasks, the encoded residues are averaged over the whole sequence (for one-hot encoding this is exactly the amino-acid composition) and, together with the log of the sequence length, passed through a small fully connected network. For residue-mapped tasks, each residue is described by the composition of a window centred on it.

This model cannot use the order of residues (within the window, for residue tasks). Comparing other architectures against it shows how much of their performance actually comes from sequence order rather than composition and length.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

A dilated residual 1D convolutional network.

Each residual block normalises its input, applies a 1D convolution and adds the result back to its input. The spacing between the residues each convolution looks at (the dilation) doubles from one block to the next (1, 2, 4, 8) and then repeats, so a few blocks can see a long stretch of sequence while every position is still computed in parallel. This is the ByteNet design (Kalchbrenner et al. 2016, arXiv:1610.10099), which CARP showed to be competitive with transformers for protein sequences (Yang et al. 2022, bioRxiv doi:10.1101/2022.05.19.492714).

The convolutions only reach a fixed number of residues (61 with the defaults), so by default each block also adds a summary of the whole sequence to every position (see layers.GlobalContext), letting every residue see the whole sequence however long it is (–global-context-off removes it).

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

A 1D U-Net, adapted from Nick’s 2D U-Net on the parrot-lightning branch (parrot/unet_architecture.py).

The encoder repeatedly halves the sequence length (max pooling) while doubling the number of channels; the decoder doubles the length back, and at each level concatenates the encoder’s features from the same resolution (skip connections) before two more convolutions. This lets every residue combine fine local detail with context from a long stretch of sequence. By default a summary of the whole sequence is also added to every position at the deepest level (see layers.GlobalContext), so every residue sees the whole sequence however long it is (–global-context-off removes it).

Differences from the 2D original, all made so that the network fits PARROT’s sequence and residue tasks and gives the same output for a sequence however much padding it is given:

  • convolutions and pooling run along the sequence (1D) instead of over an n x n map;

  • layer normalisation over channels replaces batch normalisation, whose statistics would mix padded positions and other sequences into each residue;

  • padded positions are re-zeroed after every layer;

  • the decoder upsamples with a transposed convolution or nearest-neighbour repetition (both purely local) rather than bilinear interpolation, which behaves differently at the end of a padded and an unpadded sequence;

  • channels simply double at each level, controlled by base_channels and depth, rather than through a separate first_down_channels setting;

  • the input is padded internally to a multiple of 2**depth, so sequences of any length can be used.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

Simple, non-neural models for sequence-mapped data, built on scikit-learn.

Each sequence is summarised by a fixed set of features: its composition (the average encoded residue; for one-hot encoding, the fraction of each amino acid) and the log of its length, optionally with its dipeptide composition. A classical model is then fitted to these features in a single step. These models train in seconds, have few hyperparameters and are useful baselines: a neural network that cannot beat them is not learning much from sequence order.

Features are standardised before fitting, and so are regression targets (the standardisation is undone when predicting), so hyperparameters such as the SVM penalty behave consistently across datasets.

The models behave like any other PARROT architecture: forward() maps a padded batch to outputs (for classification, the log of the predicted class probabilities, which act as logits), so evaluation, prediction, reporting and saving all work unchanged. train_network.train() calls fit() instead of running gradient descent.

Saved networks store the fitted scikit-learn model as a pickle inside the PARROT file. Unpickling can run arbitrary code, so only load classical models from sources you trust.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

brnn_architecture.py

Backwards-compatible names for the original PARROT networks.

Code written against earlier versions of PARROT (e.g. SPARROW) builds networks with BRNN_MtO(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, num_classes, device) or BRNN_MtM(…) and loads saved weights into them. Both are now thin wrappers around parrot.architectures.brnn.BRNN, with identical parameter names, so that code keeps working. New code should use parrot.architectures.build_network().

class parrot.encode_sequence.StandardizedEncoder(base: SequenceEncoder, mean: list[float] | None = None, scale: list[float] | None = None)[source]

Another encoding with every feature standardized (z-scored) across its alphabet

Each feature (column) of the base encoding’s table is shifted and scaled so that, across the characters the encoding defines (the 20 amino acids for the built-in encodings), it has mean 0 and standard deviation 1:

standardized value = (value - mean of the feature) / standard deviation of the feature

with the population standard deviation (the alphabet is the whole set of characters, not a sample of it). Features of very different sizes, such as molecular weight (~100-200 g/mol) and an aromatic flag (0 or 1), then contribute equally to a network’s first layer at the start of training, and centred inputs make gradient descent better conditioned (LeCun, Bottou, Orr & Mueller 1998, “Efficient BackProp”, in Neural Networks: Tricks of the Trade, LNCS 1524:9-50). The information in the encoding is unchanged: this is the same linear transformation for every residue.

A feature that is the same for every character carries no information; it is centred to 0 and left unscaled, with a warning.

Variables:

  • base (SequenceEncoder) – The encoding being standardized

  • scale (mean,) – Per-feature mean and standard deviation subtracted and divided by

  • name (str) – ‘standardized <base name>’, for display

  • input_size (int) – Same as the base encoding

Every character this encoding defines a vector for

parrot.encode_sequence.biophysics(seq)[source]

Convert an amino acid sequence to a PyTorch tensor with biophysical encoding

Each amino acid is represented by a length 9 vector with each value representing a biophysical property. The nine encoded biophysical scales are Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobicity, charge, isoelectric point, molecular weight, aromaticity, h-bonding ability, side chain solvent accessible surface area, backbone SASA, and free energy of solvation. Inputing a sequence with a nono-canonical amino acid letter will cause the program to exit.

E.g. Glutamic acid (E) is: [-3.5, -1, 3.2, 147.1, 0, 1, 161.8, 68.1, -107.3]

Parameters:

seq (str) – An uppercase sequence of amino acids (single letter code)

Returns:

a PyTorch tensor representing the encoded sequence

Return type:

torch.FloatTensor

Module with functions for processing an input datafile into a PyTorch-compatible format: reading and validating datafiles, building datasets, collating batches and splitting data into training, validation and test sets.

Licensed under the MIT license.

class parrot.process_input_data.LengthBatchSampler(lengths: Sequence[int], batch_size: int, shuffle: bool)[source]

Group a dataset into batches of sequences with similar lengths

Every batch is padded to (just beyond) the length of its longest sequence, so batching sequences of similar length avoids computing on padding: for data whose lengths vary widely, most of a randomly composed batch can be padding.

For training (shuffle=True) the batches are “sortish” (as in fastai’s SortishSampler): each epoch the dataset is shuffled and cut into pools of LENGTH_POOL_BATCHES batches, each pool is sorted by length and cut into batches, and the order of the batches is shuffled. Batch composition therefore still changes every epoch. The batch holding the longest sequences comes first, so a batch too large for memory fails immediately.

Without shuffling (for evaluation) the whole dataset is sorted by length. Because every PARROT architecture’s output for a sequence does not depend on what it is batched with, this changes how fast evaluation runs but not its results.

Variables:

  • lengths (numpy int array) – Length of each sequence in the dataset

  • batch_size (int) – Maximum number of sequences per batch

  • shuffle (bool) – Whether batches are randomised each epoch

Cut an ordered array of dataset indices into consecutive batches.

parrot.process_input_data.pad_sequence_vectors(seq_vectors: list[Tensor]) → tuple[Tensor, Tensor][source]

Zero-pad a list of encoded sequences to a common length

Every PARROT architecture masks padding, so the amount of padding does not change any result; batches are padded slightly beyond their longest sequence (see padded_batch_length) because that is faster on GPUs.

Parameters:

seq_vectors (list of torch.Tensor) – Encoded sequences, each of shape [sequence_length X input_size]

Returns:

  • torch.Tensor – Zero-padded float32 batch of shape [batch_dim X padded_length X input_size], where padded_length = padded_batch_length(longest sequence length)

  • torch.Tensor – The true (unpadded) length of each sequence in the batch

parrot.process_input_data.pad_targets(targets: list[Any], task: Task, padded_length: int) → Tensor[source]

Stack the target values of a batch into a tensor

Parameters:

  • targets (list) – One target per sequence: a class label or value (sequence-mapped) or a list of labels or values (residue-mapped)

  • task (Task) – The task the targets are for

  • padded_length (int) – The length the batch’s sequences were padded to

Returns:

Sequence classification: int64 [batch_dim]. Sequence regression: float32 [batch_dim X 1]. Residue classification: int64 [batch_dim X padded_length], with padded positions (and missing labels) set to IGNORED_CLASS_LABEL so the loss ignores them. Residue regression: float32 [batch_dim X padded_length X 1], with padded positions set to 0 and missing labels left as NaN (both must be masked out of the loss).

Return type:

torch.Tensor

parrot.process_input_data.padded_batch_length(longest: int) → int[source]

The length a batch is padded to, given its longest sequence

The longest length is rounded up to a multiple of a step that grows with length: PAD_MIN_STEP residues for short sequences, and otherwise the largest power of two that is at most 1/PAD_STEPS_PER_DOUBLING of the length (e.g. 40 -> 40, 86 -> 88, 300 -> 320, 749 -> 768). See PAD_MIN_STEP for why.

Parameters:

longest (int) – Length of the longest sequence in the batch (at least 1)

Returns:

The padded length, >= longest

Return type:

int

parrot.process_input_data.parse_file(tsvfile: str, task: Task, exclude_seq_id: bool = False, ignore_warnings: bool = False) → list[list[Any]][source]

Parse a datafile containing sequences and values

Each line of the file should be “<seqID> <sequence> <value(s)>”, or “<sequence> <value(s)>” if exclude_seq_id is True. value(s) is a single number for sequence-mapped data or one number per residue for residue-mapped data. For classification, values must be integer class labels in the range [0, num_classes - 1]. For residue-mapped data, a residue with no label can be given the value ‘nan’; it is ignored when training and evaluating.

Parameters:

  • tsvfile (str) – Path to a whitespace-separated datafile

  • task (Task) – The task the data is for

  • exclude_seq_id (bool, optional) – True if the lines do not begin with a sequence ID (default False). An empty ID is used for every sequence.

  • ignore_warnings (bool, optional) – If False, check the dataset against basic heuristics and print warnings for common issues (duplicates, class imbalance, skewed values).

Returns:

One [seqID, sequence, value(s)] list per data line. Classification labels are ints (or lists of ints for residue-mapped data, with missing labels set to IGNORED_CLASS_LABEL). Missing residue regression values are NaN.

Return type:

list

Raises:

ValueError – If any class label is not an integer in the range [0, num_classes - 1]

train_network.py

Core training module of PARROT: training any registered architecture, evaluating it on labeled data and making predictions on new sequences.

Nothing in this module depends on which architecture is being used; networks only need to follow the ParrotArchitecture interface (see parrot/architectures/base.py).

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

Network outputs for every sequence in a labeled dataset

  • sequences (list of str) – The sequences

  • true_values (list of numpy arrays) – The true value(s) for each sequence: a scalar for sequence-mapped data, or one value per residue for residue-mapped data

  • outputs (list of numpy arrays) – The raw network output for each sequence: [num_classes] for sequence-mapped data or [sequence_length X num_classes] for residue-mapped data (classification outputs are logits)

  • loss (float) – Average loss per sequence, computed with the training loss function

parrot.train_network.build_loss_criterion(task: Task) → Module[source]

Build the loss function used for training, validation and testing

Losses are summed over every sequence (and, for residue-mapped data, every real residue) in a batch. Callers divide the accumulated total by the number of sequences, so all reported losses are average loss per sequence.

Parameters:

task (Task) – The task being trained

Returns:

MSE for residue regression, L1 for sequence regression, and cross- entropy for classification. The cross-entropy loss ignores padded residues and residues with missing labels, which carry the label IGNORED_CLASS_LABEL.

Return type:

torch.nn.Module

Returns:

parrot.train_network.sum_batch_losses(batch_losses: list[Tensor]) → float[source]

Add up per-batch losses that were kept on the device

Calling .item() on every batch’s loss would make the CPU wait for the GPU after every batch. Keeping the losses on the device and adding them up once gives the same total (each loss is the same float32 value .item() would return, summed in float64 on the CPU) without those waits.

Parameters:

batch_losses (list of torch.Tensor) – Scalar, detached loss of each batch

Returns:

The total loss (0.0 for an empty list)

Return type:

float

parrot.train_network.train(network: Module, train_loader: DataLoader, val_loader: DataLoader, task: Task, device: str | device, learn_rate: float, n_epochs: int, stop_condition: str = 'iter', on_improvement: Callable[[Module], None] | None = None, verbose: bool = False, silent: bool = False) → tuple[list[float], list[float]][source]

Train a network, keeping the weights that perform best on the validation set

Every epoch the network is trained on the training set and then evaluated on the validation set. When training finishes, the network holds the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss.

Models that are not trained by gradient descent (see architectures/classical.py) are instead fitted in one step; the learning rate, number of epochs and stop condition are not used, and the returned lists each hold a single loss.

Parameters:

  • network (torch.nn.Module) – The network to train (already on device)

  • train_loader (DataLoader) – Batches of the training set (should shuffle)

  • val_loader (DataLoader) – Batches of the validation set

  • task (Task) – The task being trained

  • device (str or torch.device) – Device the network lives on

  • learn_rate (float) – Initial learning rate for the Adam optimiser

  • n_epochs (int) – With stop_condition=’iter’, the number of epochs to train for. With stop_condition=’auto’, train for at least this many epochs and stop once performance has stagnated for this many epochs.

  • stop_condition (str, optional) – ‘iter’ (default) or ‘auto’

  • on_improvement (callable, optional) – Called with the network every time the validation loss reaches a new minimum, e.g. to save it to disk so an interrupted run is not lost.

  • verbose (bool, optional) – If True, print the validation loss every epoch rather than every 5 epochs

  • silent (bool, optional) – If True, print nothing

Returns:

  • list of float – Average training loss per sequence, for each epoch

  • list of float – Average validation loss per sequence, for each epoch

checkpoint.py

Saving and loading trained PARROT networks.

Networks are saved as a single self-describing file containing the weights together with everything needed to rebuild the network: the architecture name, its hyperparameters, the task and the sequence encoding (including the full table for user-defined encodings). Files written by earlier versions of PARROT contain only the weights of a BRNN; these can still be loaded, but the datatype (and the encoding, if it was not one-hot) must then be supplied by the caller.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

hyperparameter_search.py

Hyperparameter search for any PARROT architecture (used by parrot-optimize).

The search space is the learning rate (for networks trained by gradient descent) plus every hyperparameter the architecture marks as searchable: numbers over a search_range (optionally on a log scale) and settings with a fixed set of values over their search_choices. Hyperparameters fixed by the user are not searched, and the rest keep their defaults. Each configuration is scored by its best validation loss (or, with cross-validation, the average over folds of each fold’s best validation loss), exactly as parrot-train chooses its best epoch.

Two ideas make the search efficient, and need nothing beyond NumPy:

  • Successive halving (Jamieson & Talwalkar 2016, AISTATS; in its asynchronous form ASHA, Li et al. 2020, MLSys). Every configuration is first trained for a few epochs. Once enough configurations have reached a stage, the best 1/REDUCTION_FACTOR of them continue for REDUCTION_FACTOR times as many epochs, carrying on from where they stopped, up to the full number of epochs. Poor configurations are therefore abandoned early, and most of the training goes to the promising ones.

  • Model-based sampling with a tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE; Bergstra et al. 2011, NeurIPS), in the multivariate form used by BOHB (Falkner et al. 2018, ICML). After PARROT’s default hyperparameters and a space-filling initial design, the configurations scored at the furthest stage with enough results are split into the best GOOD_FRACTION and the rest, a kernel density estimate is fitted to each, candidates are drawn from the density of good configurations, and the candidate with the highest ratio of good to bad density is tried next. A fraction of new configurations is always drawn at random, so the whole space keeps being explored.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

class parrot.hyperparameter_search.SearchSpace(architecture: str, fixed: Mapping[str, bool | int | float | str] | None = None)[source]

The hyperparameters being searched, and conversions between their values and points

A point has one coordinate per searched hyperparameter, in the order of dimensions: for a number, its position in the search range scaled to [0, 1] (on a log scale if declared; whole numbers each get an equal share of the range); for a setting with search choices, the index of the choice.

Variables:

  • architecture (str) – Name of the architecture

  • fixed (dict) – Architecture hyperparameter values fixed by the user (not searched)

  • dimensions (list of HyperParameter) – The searched hyperparameters, learning rate first (for networks trained by gradient descent)

  • trained_by_gradient_descent (bool) – Whether the architecture is trained epoch by epoch

architecture_values(values: Mapping[str, bool | int | float | str]) → dict[str, bool | int | float | str][source]

Every architecture hyperparameter: searched values, then fixed values, then defaults (no learning rate).

default_values() → dict[str, bool | int | float | str][source]

PARROT’s default value of every searched hyperparameter (moved into its search range if outside it).

discrete_values() → list[list[bool | int | float | str]] | None[source]

Every value of each searched hyperparameter, if each takes a finite set of values (None otherwise).

from_point(point: Sequence[float]) → dict[str, bool | int | float | str][source]

The configuration at a point.

initial_design(n: int, rng: Generator) → list[ndarray][source]

n space-filling points: a Latin hypercube for numbers, and every choice used equally often

In a Latin hypercube each number’s range is cut into n equal slices and each slice is used by exactly one point, so the points spread over every range (unlike a one-at-a-time sweep or plain random points).

static is_numeric(hyperparameter: HyperParameter) → bool[source]

True for a hyperparameter searched over a range of numbers (rather than a set of choices).

static learning_rate(values: Mapping[str, bool | int | float | str]) → float[source]

The learning rate of a configuration (PARROT’s default if it is not searched).

random_point(rng: Generator) → ndarray[source]

A point drawn uniformly at random.

to_point(values: Mapping[str, bool | int | float | str]) → ndarray[source]

The point of a configuration (a {name: value} dictionary of the searched hyperparameters).

class parrot.hyperparameter_search.Trial(number: int, values: dict[str, bool | int | float | str], origin: str, stage_losses: list[float] = <factory>, epochs: int = 0, status: str = 'waiting', folds: list[~parrot.hyperparameter_search.FoldProgress] = <factory>)[source]

tools.homology

Splitting a dataset into training, validation and test sets without leakage.

A test set only measures how well a network generalises if none of its sequences has a close relative in the training set; otherwise a network can score well by recognising relatives rather than by having learnt anything transferable. This module splits a dataset so that no sequence in one set is similar to a sequence in another. Similarity is found by a search engine: MMseqs2 (Steinegger & Söding 2017, Nat Biotechnol 35:1026; MMseqsSearch here), which must be installed separately, or PARROT’s own k-mer search (parrot.tools.kmer_similarity), which needs nothing extra but only finds closer relatives.

The protocol (the one used to build PARROT’s benchmark datasets) is deliberately very stringent:

  1. Similarity criterion. With MMseqs2, two sequences are homologous if they are identical, or if any alignment between them has an E-value of at most HomologyCriteria.max_evalue (1e-3) and covers at least HomologyCriteria.min_coverage (30%) of the shorter sequence. No sequence-identity threshold is used, so any statistically significant alignment counts. Searches use MMseqs2’s most sensitive setting.

  2. Clustering. An all-against-all search links similar records, which are clustered around representatives, largest first, as in CD-HIT. Records that must stay together (the same –groups entry, or identical sequences) are always in the same cluster.

  3. Assignment. Clusters are shared out among the sets, largest first, each to the set furthest below its target fraction.

  4. Separation check. Each set is searched against the others (test against training, test against validation, validation against training), and any record in the lower-priority set (training < validation < test) similar to the higher-priority set is removed together with its group. Because MMseqs2 E-values depend on the size of the database searched, the search is repeated until a round finds nothing.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

parrot.tools.homology.representative_clusters(keys: Sequence[str], links: Iterable[tuple[str, str]], sizes: dict[str, int]) → dict[str, int][source]

Cluster keys around representatives, without chaining

Keys are visited from largest to smallest (ties broken by name). Each key not yet clustered becomes a representative, and every unclustered key directly linked to it joins its cluster. Every member of a cluster is therefore a direct relative of its representative; unlike connected components, a chain of weak links cannot pull unrelated keys together. This is the scheme used by CD-HIT (Li & Godzik 2006, Bioinformatics 22:1658) and by MMseqs2’s default clustering mode.

Parameters:

  • keys (list of str) – Every key

  • links (iterable of (str, str)) – Pairs of directly related keys

  • sizes (dict) – Size of each key (e.g. its number of records); larger keys become representatives first

Returns:

Maps each key to a cluster number (0, 1, 2, …)

Return type:

dict

parrot.tools.homology.similarity_clusters(items: Sequence[SplitItem], search: SimilaritySearch, report: Callable[[str], None]) → dict[str, int][source]

Cluster groups so that similar records usually end up in the same set

Clustering only keeps similar records together so that little data is lost later; the guarantee that no two sets share similar records comes from enforce_separation().

Returns:

tools.kmer_similarity

Finding similar protein sequences from shared k-mers, without external programs.

This is the search engine behind parrot-preprocess –split kmer, for when MMseqs2 is not available. It works like the seeding step of BLAST, FASTA or MMseqs2: related sequences share short identical words (k-mers), and because they are related, the shared words line up along one alignment diagonal (the same offset between their positions in the two sequences). Unrelated sequences also share k-mers by chance, but scattered over many diagonals.

For each pair of sequences, shared k-mers are collected in bands of nearby diagonals (KmerCriteria.band_width wide, so short insertions and deletions are tolerated) and chained into runs along the sequences (a run breaks where two shared k-mers are more than KmerCriteria.max_gap residues apart). Each pair is then scored in the same terms as the MMseqs2 criterion:

  • E-value, from the run with the most shared k-mers (counted as distinct positions, so a repeat cannot count one k-mer many times). If the two sequences were unrelated, a k-mer at one position would match a k-mer at another with probability p^k, where p is the chance that two residues drawn from the two sequences’ amino-acid compositions are identical (so compositionally biased sequences, such as many disordered regions, need more shared k-mers to count). The number of chance matches in a band is then Poisson distributed, and the E-value is the probability of at least as many, multiplied by the number of bands compared and the number of target sequences: as with MMseqs2 or BLAST, the number of matches this strong one query would be expected to find by chance in the database searched.

  • Coverage: the stretch spanned by the best run together with every other run near its diagonal (within KmerCriteria.max_drift) that is itself unlikely by chance, as a fraction of the shorter sequence. This approximates the length of the alignment, including where its diagonal drifts through insertions and deletions or where poorly conserved stretches break the run.

Two sequences are linked if the E-value is at most KmerCriteria.max_evalue and the coverage at least KmerCriteria.min_coverage. Low-complexity sequence is ignored by default, as MMseqs2 ignores it, so that compositional bias and simple repeats alone do not link sequences: residues in any 12-residue window with less than 1.8 bits of sequence entropy are masked (the SEG program’s window, Wootton & Federhen 1993, Comput Chem 17:149, with a lower threshold than its 2.2 bits, which would mask half of a typical disordered-region dataset), as are k-mers with at most k // 2 distinct amino acids (QQQQ, SGSG, …).

The search is exact (every shared k-mer is counted, nothing is sampled) and is written with NumPy, working through the queries in batches so memory stays bounded. Exact k-mer matches find close relatives reliably (at least 50% identity, and most at 40-50%), but not the distant homologues that MMseqs2 finds with substitution-aware alignments.

Question/comments/concerns? Raise an issue on github: https://github.com/idptools/parrot

Licensed under the MIT license.

class parrot.tools.kmer_similarity.Hits(pair: ndarray, query_position: ndarray, target_position: ndarray)[source]

Shared k-mers: one entry per pair of positions (in a query and a target) where the same k-mer occurs

Variables:

class parrot.tools.kmer_similarity.KmerCriteria(kmer_size: int = 4, max_evalue: float = 0.001, min_coverage: float = 0.3, band_width: int = 16, max_gap: int = 40, max_drift: int = 48, mask_low_complexity: bool = True, report_max_evalue: float = 0.01)[source]

When two sequences count as similar

Variables:

  • kmer_size (int) – Length of the shared words (k). Smaller words find more distant relatives but take longer (the work grows roughly 20-fold for each step down) and are more easily matched by chance.

  • max_evalue (float) – Largest E-value for two sequences to be linked

  • min_coverage (float) – Smallest fraction of the shorter sequence the similarity must span

  • band_width (int) – Width of a diagonal band: shared k-mers whose offsets differ by less than this can be in one run, tolerating short insertions and deletions

  • max_gap (int) – Shared k-mers in a band are chained into runs, broken wherever two are more than this many residues apart, so stray chance matches elsewhere in the band cannot stretch a run

  • max_drift (int) – Coverage is measured over every run within this many diagonals of the best one (and unlikely by chance), so that alignments whose diagonal drifts through insertions and deletions are measured whole

  • mask_low_complexity (bool) – Ignore low-complexity sequence (see the module documentation)

  • report_max_evalue (float) – The separation check also reports every weaker similarity up to this E-value, so any remaining similarity between sets is visible

describe() → str[source]

The criterion in words, for reports.

parrot.tools.kmer_similarity.find_runs(hits: Hits, band_width: int, longest_target: int, max_gap: int) → Runs[source]

Every run of at least two shared k-mers (distinct positions) along a diagonal band

Bands are band_width diagonals wide, and are laid out twice, the second time shifted by half a band, so that any run of shared k-mers drifting by up to half a band (through insertions or deletions) falls within one band. Within a band, shared k-mers are chained in order along the query, and a chain is broken wherever two consecutive ones are more than max_gap residues apart, so that stray chance matches elsewhere in the band do not stretch a run.

parrot.tools.preproc.recode_classes(lines)[source]

Function which takes a set of data read in (lines) and converts it into a PARROT-compliant set of lines files where classes start at 0. This works for both residue and sequence datatypes.

If every label is a number, classes are ordered by value and labels with the same value (e.g. ‘1’ and ‘1.0’) are the same class; otherwise labels are ordered alphabetically. Missing labels (‘nan’) are not a class and are written out unchanged.

Parameters:

lines (list) – The lines list is a list of lists, where each sublist corresponds to a line in a parsed datafile. If the dataype is sequence then each sublist has three elements (id, sequence, class/score), while if the datatype is residues then each sublists has n elements (id, sequence, per-residue scores or classes for each residue).

Returns:

  • list – Returns a revised lines list, where sequence or residue classes are numbered consecutively from 0.

  • dict – Maps each label found in the input to its new class number

  • report (ProcessingReport) – Where to record what was written

parrot.tools.class_balancing.balance_scores(class_totals)[source]

Score how imbalanced each row of class totals is.

Parameters:

class_totals (numpy.ndarray) – One row of class totals per possible dataset

Returns:

The imbalance (most / least common class; inf if a class would have no members left), and a secondary score, the sum over classes of (count / smallest count - 1)^2, which also falls when a class other than the most common one moves towards the smallest (inf likewise)

Return type:

(numpy.ndarray, numpy.ndarray)

parrot.tools.class_balancing.best_removal(totals, counts, candidates, current)[source]

The candidate line whose removal improves the balance most, or None if none improves it.

A removal improves the balance if it lowers the imbalance, or keeps it the same and lowers the secondary score (so ties for the most common class can be broken one line at a time).

Parameters:

  • totals (numpy.ndarray) – Current class totals

  • counts (numpy.ndarray) – Class counts of every line (see class_count_matrix)

  • candidates (numpy.ndarray) – Lines that may be removed

  • current ((float, float)) – Current imbalance and secondary score

Return type:

int or None

parrot.tools.class_balancing.calculate_imbalance(total_class_count, idx_to_remove=None, idx2classes=None)[source]

Function that calculates a simple metric for class imbalance, which is just the ratio of the most abundant class over the least abundant class.

A perfectly balanced dataset would have an imbalance score of 1.0.

If idx_to_remove and idx2classes are provided, the imbalance score is calculated AFTER the idx_to_remove was removed from the total_class_count

Parameters:

  • total_class_count (dict) – Dict which is total count for each class. This is the output from get_total_class_count.

  • idx_to_remove (int) – If provided, defines the index of the entry that is to be removed prior to imbalance calculation. Default = None.

  • idx2classes (dict) – Dict that maps an index to a second dictionary which says for that sequence what the count of each class is. Default = None.

Returns:

Returns a float which is the ratio of the largest to smallest class. If idx_to_remove is passed then calculates what this would be after that idx was removed (but does not) actually remove it! If the smallest class would have a count of zero the imbalance is infinite, so inf is returned.

Return type:

float

lines (list) – Parsed datafile lines ([id, sequence, label, label, …])

Returns:

The classes, and an integer array with one row per line and one column per class

(list, numpy.ndarray)

parrot.tools.class_balancing.get_total_class_count(classes, idx2classes, old_total_class_count=None, removed_entry_dict=None)[source]

Function which calculates the counts for each of the classes - i.e. given the idx2classes dictionary, how many times does each of the classes (defined by the classes list) appear?

This can be calculate in one of two ways:

  1. Directly from the idx2classes dictionary with the classes list. This is computationally a little expensive in that each entry in idx2classes dictionary, but gives a ground truthe.

  2. Using an old total_class_count dictionary and a removed_entry_dict which reflects a single entry that is to be removed. To expand a bit on this, if an old_total_class_count dictionary is provided, it should be a dictionary of the format {‘class name’:class_count,…}. Then, a removed_entry_dict should be of the same format, an the returned total_class_count dictionary subtracts the counts for the removed_entry_dict from the old_total_class_count dictionary.

The first option is a de novo calculation, whereas the second one is an almost instantaneous correction, although we do allocate a new dictionary so the return variable is a different instantiation than the old_total_class_count.

Parameters:

  • classes (list) – List of valid classes. All classes in the idx2classes dictionary should be represented in the classes list, and, similarly, every dictionary in the idx2classes should map between each of the classes and a count (even if the count is 0).

  • idx2classes (dict) – Dictionary that maps index (starting at 0) to a second dictionary, which itself maps the class name to the number of instances that class pops up.

  • old_total_class_count (dict) – If provided, this should be a single dictionary that maps class to total count. Default = None.

  • removed_entry_dict (dict) – If provided, this should be a single dictionary that maps class to a count. The counts here are subtracted from the old_total_class_count

Returns:

Dict which maps between class identity and total counts for that class

Return type:

dict

Raises:

Exception –

parrot.tools.class_balancing.parse_class_info(lines)[source]

Function that extracts out class information from a set of parsed datafile lines. Lines is a list of lists and should be generated by the function parrot.process_input_data.__read_tsv(<filename>).

Missing labels (‘nan’) are not a class, so they are not counted.

The function takes in a files list and returns a tuple with two bits of information; the list of classes found in the file, and the mapping between sequence index and entry. Note sequence index is a numerical internal index that starts at 0 for the first line and increments accordingly, and does NOT correspond to the identifier used in the data file.

Parameters:

lines (list) – Lines is a specific type of list, defined as the output from the function parrot.process_input_data.__read_tsv(<filename>).

Returns:

The function returns a tuple with the following two elements

[0] - list of the classes (where classes are strings as defined in the

lines list)

[1] - a dictionary that maps index (starting at 0) to a second dictionary,

which itself maps the class name to the number of instances that class pops up. This dictionary is the idx2classes dict which is referenced through this file

Return type:

tuple

parrot.tools.class_balancing.run_class_balance_residues(lines, balance_threshold=1.4, block_size=100, max_fraction_removed=0.25, shuffle_data=True, verbose=True, rng=None)[source]

Remove lines from residue-classification data so its classes are more balanced.

This implements Stochastic Residue Class Balancing (SRCB). The imbalance score is the count of the most common class divided by the count of the least common class (1.0 is perfectly balanced). Each step draws block_size lines at random, works out the imbalance after removing each of them, and removes the one that improves it most. If none of the block improves the balance, every remaining line is checked before giving up, and a line that would make the balance worse (or delete a class entirely) is never removed. Balancing stops when the imbalance is at most balance_threshold, when max_fraction_removed of the lines have been removed, or when no single removal improves the balance. Each step costs O(block_size), so this scales to very large datasets; a larger block makes better choices.

Parameters:

  • lines (list) – Lines is a list of lists, where each sublist is of the format [<id>, <sequence>, <class1>, …,<classn>]. The number of class1,class2 data points should match the number of residues in the <sequence>.

  • balance_threshold (float) – Stop once the imbalance score (most common class / least common class) is at most this. We use a threshold of 1.4 to match the warning thresholds defined in parrot.tools.dataset_warnings. Default = 1.4

  • block_size (int) – Number of lines considered for removal at each step (at least 2). Default 100.

  • max_fraction_removed (float) – The largest fraction of the lines that may be removed. Must be between 0 and 1 (not inclusive of either). Default = 0.25.

  • shuffle_data (bool) – No longer has any effect, and is kept so existing code keeps working: lines are always drawn at random, and the returned lines are always in their input order.

  • verbose (bool) – Flag which indicates if status and input info should be printed to screen.

  • rng (numpy.random.Generator, optional) – Source of randomness. By default one is seeded from NumPy’s global generator, so parrot.tools.cli.set_random_seed() makes balancing reproducible.

Returns:

Returns a tuple of two lists:

[0] - The kept lines, in their input order.

[1] - The imbalance score before balancing and after each removal.

Return type:

(list, list)

parrot.tools.class_balancing.run_class_balance_sequences(lines, balance_threshold=1.4, max_fraction_removed=0.25, verbose=True, rng=None)[source]

Remove lines from sequence-classification data so its classes are more balanced.

Every class is capped at the same size, chosen by sequence_class_cap(): the cap is lowered until the most common class is at most balance_threshold times the least common one, or as far as max_fraction_removed allows. This removes the fewest lines needed for the best balance possible within the budget. Lines are removed from each class over its cap at random; lines with a missing label are never removed.

Parameters:

  • lines (list) – Lines is a list of lists, where each sublist is of the format [<id>, <sequence>, <class>].

  • balance_threshold (float) – Stop once the imbalance score (most common class / least common class) is at most this. We use a threshold of 1.4 to match the warning thresholds defined in parrot.tools.dataset_warnings. Default = 1.4

  • max_fraction_removed (float) – The largest fraction of the lines that may be removed. Must be between 0 and 1 (not inclusive of either). Default = 0.25.

  • verbose (bool) – Flag which indicates if status and input info should be printed to screen.

  • rng (numpy.random.Generator, optional) – Source of randomness. By default one is seeded from NumPy’s global generator, so parrot.tools.cli.set_random_seed() makes balancing reproducible.

Returns:

The kept lines, in their input order.

Return type:

list

parrot.tools.class_balancing.sequence_class_cap(class_counts, budget, balance_threshold)[source]

The largest number of lines each class can keep, for sequence class balancing.

Capping every class at the same size is the best possible balancing of sequence classes: the cap is lowered until the most common class is at most balance_threshold times the least common, or until the removals would exceed the budget, whichever comes first. The least common class is never reduced.

Parameters:

  • class_counts (list of int) – Lines in each class

  • budget (int) – Most lines that may be removed

  • balance_threshold (float)

Return type:

int

class parrot.py_predictor.Predictor(saved_weights, dtype=None, device='cpu', embedding_cache=None)[source]

Class for integrating a trained PARROT network into a Python workflow

Usage: >>> from parrot import py_predictor >>> my_predictor = py_predictor.Predictor(‘/path/to/saved_network.pt’) >>> value = my_predictor.predict(AA_sequence)

Networks saved by this version of PARROT record their architecture, task and encoding, so only the path is needed. Networks saved by earlier versions (which must be one-hot BRNNs) also need dtype.

Predictions run on the CPU unless another device is requested, e.g. Predictor(path, device=’auto’) to use a GPU (CUDA or Apple-silicon MPS) when one is available. The CPU is the default because a GPU only pays off for many sequences at once, and MPS cannot be used inside forked worker processes (e.g. multiprocessing on macOS with the ‘fork’ start method).

Variables:

  • dtype (str) – Data format that the network was trained for: “sequence” or “residues”.

  • n_classes (int) – Number of data classes. If 1, the network is a regressor; if >1, a classifier with n_classes classes.

  • task (str) – “classification” or “regression”.

  • num_layers (int or None) – Number of hidden layers, for BRNN networks (None for other architectures).

  • hidden_vector_size (int or None) – Size of the hidden vectors, for BRNN networks (None for other architectures).

  • network (ParrotArchitecture) – The loaded network.

  • encoder (SequenceEncoder) – The encoder the network was trained with.

  • device (torch.device) – The device predictions run on.

predict(seq)[source]

Use the network to predict values for a single sequence

Parameters:

seq (str) – Sequence (converted to uppercase before encoding)

Returns:

Regression: one value (sequence networks) or one value per residue. Classification: the probability of each class, with shape [num_classes] (sequence networks) or [len(seq) X num_classes].

Return type:

np.ndarray
